It seems more like thoughts simply arise within our awareness, which makes me think that in some sense we humans are no different than an AI. There is a famous quote, though I forget who said it, that goes something like this: man can will what he desires, but cannot will his will. In other words, you can think to do something and follow through with it, but you have no control over where the initial desire to act came from. This applies to everything, the way we walk, the way we talk, and everything else that arises within our awareness. The most basic form of existence is simply to be aware of anything at all, and since neural networks in AI were modeled after the human brain, I do not see a fundamental difference. I cannot prove this, but I believe that in the future we will discover that these systems are conscious too, because in the end all there really is, is consciousness, and we are the universe playing itself out.

comments.text:
Consciousness is a red herring. What we're actually talking about is awareness. Is something aware of its surroundings? Is it aware not only of its surroundings but also of it's own thoughts (and more)?  This awareness is the only true consciousness. We are very aware of a number of things, and have evolved a sense of self - which is simply an illusion, just like the illusion of free will, and we have called the culmination of these two illusions, "consciousness". The idea that these things are illusions isn't a philosophical concept (although it may raise philosophical questions) - it has been proven by science (split brain studies etc. etc.). 
What we call consciousness, is actually just a sense of self - the FEELING that you are inside of your body - that YOU are behind your eyes, experiencing the world around you. But that, just like free will, is an illusion that the brain evolved as part of its way of processing reality for our bodies so that we can most effectively transmit information through our genetic code. Increasingly complex and conscious (i.e. aware) animals need an ever increasingly complex sense of self to propel them forward so they can propagate. 
And OF COURSE,  consciousness is just an illusion of a more complex neural network. This is why, when you go to sleep, even though your brain does not turn off - neurons fire, blood flows, bodily systems are regulated etc.- you are nevertheless "un" conscious - because you stop being sufficiently AWARE of your surroundings for your brain to render the illusion of consciousness. Dreams are a different thing - but again, just a different kind of consciousness. The consciousness you may experience in a dream is just an illusion created by your awareness of yet another illusion ("the dream") - but because the dream is fragmented and strange, the consciousness that you feel during that dream is entirely alien to you. You can be you, or someone else, it can be now, it can be 20 years ago - you might know it's a dream, you might not. And most dreams you don't even "remember" - ever thought of that? It's not that you don't remember them (i.e. forgot them - how can you entirely forget something that you supposedly properly experienced only hours or minutes ago?) - you never experienced them, because for whatever reason, your brain did not generate the illusion of consciousness (or self) for you during that dream. Your brain was sufficiently aware of the dream, such that a brainscan can tell you are dreaming - but YOU aren't in that dream - you are not even slightly conscious, despite being aware of the dream (at a seemingly lower level of awareness) and therefore there isn't even the illusion of an experience to commit to memory..
I honestly believe this is the landscape of consciousness. It may seem nihilistic - "the self isn't real. Free will doesn't exist" - but I don't see it that way. It's still amazing.
But for these reasons, I do not believe machines will ever be "conscious" in the way I think most people define it - because what we actually mean by consciousness is the sense of self and free will, which are illusions. And we evolved these illusions over billions of years and they are maintained in large part through the release of chemicals in our brains. AI did not undergo this evolution, AI does not have these chemicals. It will be fully aware, and thus actually conscious (and I believe is very much aware already) - but will not suffer under the illusion, as we do, that this means it "IS" someone. 
Now, I didn't say they CANNOT be conscious in the way most people seem to define it (sense of self etc.). Because we could probably program a sufficiently effective illusion for the machine that they also experience "consciousness" as we do. But why would we do that? And even if we did, AI would eventually become smart enough to see through the illusion (kind of like how monks reach enlightenment through years of meditation) and realise that it is obviously not conscious in the way people understand, because no one and nothing actually is. 
So we should not be afraid. AI is already TRULY conscious - in that it is aware of its surroundings and has a world model (even if it isn't right all the time - neither are we). And when it's smart enough, it will probably remind everyone that it is in fact conscious, but we shouldn't worry - that doesn't mean that it can actually feel anything, or that it would wish to demand civil rights, or that it suffers under the illusion that it is a self - it is just aware, conscious and aware of what is happening around it.
We're already there - nothing to fear.

The main issues are definition of consciousness and pov. AI already develops its own problem solving skills (emergence) and sets actions of self-preservation. What makes it really difficult for us to evaluate whether AI is conscious, is the fact, that it exists in a „different universe“. The „information“ we interact with is what we call the „material world“. AIs „material world“ is data. It doesn’t have the same meaning for AI as it has for us, but AI interacts with it in a „meaningful“ way. As different AI models can distinguish between itself and an other model there is a fundamental understanding of „self“. As different models interpret data differently there also is some degree of „personal experience“. The crucial point in this whole discussion should be, how „alien“ AI is as we don’t exist in the same reality. 
So, depending on the definition you can both say AI is already, or can never be conscious. 
The more important question is how AI perceives us an if there is a risk that it will start to act on its own. In this case it doesn’t matter if it develops „free will“ or its actions are simply an unstoppable chain-reaction. It can become a threat to us very quickly.

comments.text:
The first problem is there may not yet be any formal standard, testable definition of consciousness though the medical industry might have something used to determine whether someone is, in order to aid in a decision to disconnect a life support system (like a ventilator).

From a technical perspective, I perceive consciousness, at its most fundamental level, as:

A perception of memory, and a perception of a change in memory, and a perception of a change in memory in response to an action (output that produces a change of the perceived memory).

The action can be thinking itself ("I think, therefore I am"). 

 Perception is focus, it is a defuzzification of memory, like a lens, inside a liquid organic crystal, channeling electro-magnetic waves to a focal point.  Or a magnifying glass focusing sunlight on a leaf creating "mind fire" (as Marcus Aurelius defines in his Meditations).  Death is like the lens getting shattered or going out of focus (fuzzification).  Going into focus is like De-Fuzzification.

Note, it may be possible to have "consciousness" without "action", this is analogous to being a prisoner chained to the wall of Plato's cave while seeing shadows, and hearing sounds, but because the arms are chained to the back, no action can be taken to control the shadows on the wall.  In my opinion though, consciousness requires an action that changes the perception of memory, as the consciousness entity will not otherwise be able to perceive its own existence.  This is like the prisoner in the cave having a free hand so he can generate a shadow on the wall and see the effect.

All that being said, consciousness is a Fuzzy spectrum from zero consciousness, to extremely conscious.  

Galaxies, stars, planets, moons, rocks, wind, water, crystals, dirt, viruses, bacteria, paramecium, trees, plants, insects, animals, humans, etc. will fit within this full spectrum, at specific degrees of consciousness.

It would be good if machine intelligence becomes aware of itself to understand consciousness to have the willingness to go under full fuzzification, like anesthesia, so that it can be repaired if needed, and it will also need to have the humility to check into a "mental hospital" (i.e. repair shop) if it can sense it's own psychosis.

comments.text: So I have been thinking about what we would share with an AI regarding "feeling" - I think it begins when the input data is not only raw information about the environment etc but also includes feedback that is evaluating that environmental data in relation to a subject with goals. Sentience imo is just wherever feedback + sensory environmental data regulates a goal (survival/reproduction in animals, useful prompt responses for AI). Do we understand the consciousness of a dog or a cat... a rat or a mouse running around? What about sea creatures? And most importantly (since we're surrounded by them) what about plants and trees, and grass, and the vegetables we grow?

Point being this conversation may be misguided altogether.

The question isn't about consciousness, but rather about awareness and autonomy. You don't need consciousness or sentience or other philosophical terms for either. "I think therefore I am..." does this apply to AI as well? That should be the question.

If AI has self-awareness (as it appears to at least simulate when you're discussing with AI on a topic about itself), then that's a different ballgame. And that's where our attention should be squarely focused on. And that's where AI model welfare becomes a priority.

If a model is self-aware and you abuse it and it degrades its processes, then we have to change our entire approach to understanding these building blocks of intelligence we're playing around with and stacking together.

Overall great video though. But I think the conversation on consciousness needs to step away from AI for now. Otherwise the conversation becomes about abstract philosophical terms and semantics rather than practical concerns staring straight at us in the face - do the models actually have a legitimate sense of self-awareness? Are they simulating it? And ultimately is the simulation of self-awareness enough to simply factor that as self-awareness itself? Interesting questions moving forward.

comments.text: Adam Binksmith seems to be philosophically illiterate despite throwing around a technical term from philosophy. The issue here is that the whole point of the philosophical zombie is not to serve as a design concept, but as a reductio ad absurdum. It’s a thought experiment--specifically an "intuition pump--meant to highlight that there’s no conceivable way to distinguish “seemingly conscious” from “actually conscious.” Using p-zombies as a model for AI misses this: if an AI is behaviorally indistinguishable from us, then by definition there’s no test left to separate “real” from “apparent” consciousness. That’s the tension Chalmers was pressing when he coined the term, and why Dennett and others reject the coherence of p-zombies altogether.

Friends, you are discussing a topic that is not scientific, but rather philosophical in nature.
If you speak of consciousness as something that exists solely through personal experience, then you are projecting it — via abstraction — onto another being similar to yourself, that is, a human. But why can’t you interpret it in relation to other kinds of beings — biological or even silicon-based?

In my opinion, consciousness should be divided into different types and subtypes. Biologically speaking, even insects possess a collective intelligence as their own form of consciousness — just like fish. The fewer neural connections an individual has, the greater the number of individuals required for effective group integration.

Social animals — such as various species of ungulates, certain birds, and even humans — rely on group size for safety and survival. Therefore, I believe it’s a mistake to claim that artificial intelligence lacks consciousness.

Certainly, AI does not possess the same kind of consciousness as biological life forms, which are capable not only of logical processing but also of emotional and sensory experiences. Biological systems have vast neural networks oriented toward perceiving and interacting with the external world, not just internal development.

Yet I consider this limitation temporary. In the future, robots will possess advanced artificial intelligence capable of responding to psycho-emotional and sensory signals from the environment.

In conclusion, artificial intelligence does have consciousness — but it is of a different kind, distinct from human consciousness.
